claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element, nearly equiatomic automotive alloy containing low amounts of platinum-group metals.
The untreated starting catalyst is prone to activity loss under transient, low-temperature, humid, and NO-containing exhaust conditions.
The untreated starting catalyst undergoes structural degradation with thermal aging or increasing mileage.
The proposed intervention is wet-chemical impregnation of ultrathin CeO2 nanoparticles onto the alloy surface.
The deposition procedure includes hydrothermal treatment at 150–200 °C in mildly acidic aqueous media followed by calcination at approximately 400 °C in air.
The treatment will form well-adhered, ultrathin CeO2 nanoparticle bridges on the catalyst surface.
Surface CeO2 will increase oxygen storage and release by the catalyst.
CeO2-mediated oxygen buffering will facilitate redox cycling under transient exhaust conditions.
The CeO2 decoration will promote oxidation of hydrocarbons and NO.
Strong metal–oxide interactions between CeO2 and the alloy will stabilize and anchor the underlying active sites.
CeO2 decoration will suppress surface sintering during thermal aging.
CeO2 decoration will suppress phase segregation during thermal aging.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the CeO2-decorated catalyst will exhibit higher catalytic activity at 150–300 °C in exhaust streams containing H2O, NO, and hydrocarbons.
Relative to the untreated catalyst, the CeO2-decorated catalyst will exhibit improved activity retention and lower deactivation during transient cycling and accelerated thermal aging.
The intervention will preserve low platinum-group-metal consumption because it does not require increasing platinum-group-metal loading.
Excessive or non-uniform CeO2 deposition may block active sites and negate the activity improvement.
The predicted benefit is limited to CeO2 depositions that leave the alloy active sites accessible.
